claims.text: Tempered martensitic steel can be used to create a spatially controlled ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
Localized induction heating can induce temper embrittlement in tempered martensitic steel.
Impurity segregation at grain boundaries is responsible for the proposed temper embrittlement.
The initial uniformly tempered martensitic steel has typical room-temperature ductility.
Heating a target zone to approximately 300°C for 25 minutes followed by slow cooling is an appropriate treatment for producing the proposed transition.
Temper embrittlement is activated within a narrow intermediate-temperature window.
Phosphorus and tin are examples of impurities that segregate to grain boundaries under the proposed conditions.
Localized thermal treatment causes impurity segregation at grain boundaries in the heated zone.
Grain-boundary impurity segregation reduces intergranular cohesion.
Reduced intergranular cohesion causes embrittlement at intermediate temperatures.
Controlled cooling modifies the impurity-segregation profile.
Modification of the segregation profile during cooling restores ductility outside the embrittled condition or zone.
Localized heated regions will undergo a significant loss of ductility within the targeted temperature range.
The embrittled regions will revert to ductile behavior as temperature is reduced further.
Untreated regions will remain mechanically distinguishable from the locally heated regions.
The proposed phenomenon is restricted to conventional alloys in which temper-embrittlement mechanisms are active.
Compositionally complex and high-entropy alloys do not exhibit the proposed temper-embrittlement effect.
